title: The Five-Model Comparator
text:
Pick a single engagement below — how many people it replaces, how much work it does, how much value it creates — then watch what the customer pays each month under every pricing model valid for your deployment tier. Nothing about the product changes between the bars. Only the commercial model changes.
Not every model is available everywhere: the CoE reference doc’s Tier-to-Model Mapping (§5.4) restricts each deployment tier to a specific subset of the five models. Change the deployment tier below and watch bars appear and disappear accordingly.
The dashed line is what the customer pays for the humans today. Anything below it is a saving you can share; anything above it needs a very good value story.

title: The Five-Model Comparator
The Five-Model Comparator
section: What the customer pays each month — and what the vendor keeps

title: The Five-Model Comparator
text:
The detail

Inputs.table(prices.map(d => ({
  Model: d.model,
  "Monthly (£)": gbp(d.price),
  "Vendor cost (£)": gbp(d.cost),
  "Profit (£)": gbp(d.profit),
  "Margin": (d.marginPct * 100).toFixed(0) + "%",
  "vs human": (d.price / humanMonthly * 100).toFixed(0) + "%",
  Basis: d.note
})), {rows: 6, layout: "auto"})

title: The Five-Model Comparator
text:
How each bar is calculated
The risk and autonomy settings apply on top of M1, M2 and M4 as a single overlay — this is the framework’s “apply the premium on top of the model price” rule:
\[\text{overlay}(x) = x \times \big(1 + \text{risk premium}\big) \times \text{autonomy modifier}\]
where the risk premium runs from +5% (score 1) to +100% (score 10), and the autonomy modifier is ×1.00 up to L3, ×1.20 at L4, and ×1.40 at L5.







Model
Monthly price (before overlay)




M1 Per Seat
\(\text{FTEs} \times \dfrac{\text{FTE cost}}{12} \times \text{seat discount}\)


M2 Usage (Tier 1)
\(\dfrac{\text{Infra} + \text{License} + \text{Support} + \text{Risk Reserve} + \text{CoE Overhead}}{1 - \text{margin}}\)


M2 Usage (Tier 2)
\((\text{volume} \times \text{calls/task}) \times \Big[\dfrac{\text{unit cost} + \text{allocated overhead}}{1 - \text{margin}} + \text{risk premium}\Big]\)


M3 Task
\(\text{volume} \times \Big[(\text{hours} \times \text{hourly rate}) \times \text{complexity} + \text{risk premium}\Big]\)


M4 Hybrid
\(\text{base fee} + \text{value} \times \text{share \%}\)


M5 Outcome
\(\max\big(\text{floor},\ \min(\text{ceiling},\ \text{value} \times \text{share \%})\big)\)



M2 has two personalities, and the deployment tier picks between them automatically. In Tier 1 it’s a flat internal cost-recovery number (no risk term of its own, so it does take the overlay) — notice it doesn’t move at all when you change the volume slider. In Tier 2 it’s a true per-unit usage price that scales with volume, and — like M3 — it carries its own risk premium, so it skips the generic overlay to avoid double-counting risk. M2 isn’t offered at all in Tier 3, so its fine-tune sliders simply have no bar to affect there.
M3 follows the same logic as M2 Tier 2: it’s the CoE reference doc’s task-pricing formula directly, with its own per-task risk premium, rather than the generic risk/autonomy overlay used by M1, M4 and M2 Tier 1. Applying the overlay and a per-unit/per-task risk premium would price risk twice.
M5 uses guardrails instead of the overlay: the floor is 80% of the (overlaid) M4 base fee — protecting your cost recovery — and the ceiling is a multiple of that floor, capping the customer’s exposure. Push the business value slider up and watch M5 climb off its floor, then slam into its ceiling: that is the whole story of outcome-based pricing in one slider.






These numbers are illustrative





The constants here are chosen to teach the shape of each model, not to quote a deal. Real engagements need the CoE templates, an audited baseline, and the token-distribution work from the next module.

title: Causal Map
text:
Every fix in this lab so far has come from tracing a chain of dependencies that wasn’t visible until something broke: volume meaning different things for different models, a mean-based price sitting next to a P90-based cost, a “risk score” that only touches three of the five models. This page draws that map out up front.
The full picture was one dense diagram; it’s split into two smaller ones below — drivers (the qualitative/shared inputs) and computation (how those drivers turn into price, cost and margin) — so each stays readable on its own.

title: Causal Map
text:
Known gaps (dashed edges above)
These are places the model treats inputs as independent when a real pricing conversation probably wouldn’t — flagged here rather than fixed, since each is a judgement call about how much realism this teaching tool needs versus how many more sliders it should have.







Gap
What’s missing




Task complexity → Token CoV
m3Complexity scales M3’s price, but has no effect on either model’s token-cost variability, even though a more complex task plausibly has a fatter-tailed token distribution too.


Risk score → per-unit risk premiums
The shared riskScore slider drives the generic overlay (M1, M2 T1, M4), but M2 Tier 2 and M3 have their own, entirely independent risk-premium sliders. Moving the shared risk score does nothing to them.


Token CoV / P90 → M5’s floor
token-distribution.qmd explicitly teaches “set the floor on the P90/P95 cost, not a flat percentage” — but M5’s actual floor is 0.8 × M4 base fee, with no connection to any token-cost distribution at all.


Deployment tier → default recalibration
Switching tiers changes which models are shown, but doesn’t adjust any default slider values — a Tier 3 (Digital Labor) scenario and a Tier 1 (Internal Use) scenario keep the same defaults even though the underlying engagement shape is usually very different.

title: Token Distribution & the P90 Floor
text:
Token cost per task is not a number — it’s a long-tailed distribution. Most runs are cheap; a few are wildly expensive. If you set your price off the mean, the tail of expensive runs eats your margin on a large share of tasks.
This app simulates that. Set the shape of the distribution, then compare two pricing strategies — price off the mean vs. price off the P90 floor (P90 cost × 1.15, the framework rule) — and watch the Monte-Carlo loss rates.

title: Token Distribution & the P90 Floor
text:
What you’re seeing
The Coefficient of Variation (CoV) is the standard deviation of cost-per-task divided by its mean — a unitless measure of how spread out costs are relative to their average. It arises here because agentic token consumption is inherently uneven: most tasks resolve in a short, cheap call, but some spiral into long tool-use chains, retries, or context-heavy prompts that cost many times more. A CoV near 0 would mean every task costs about the same (the mean is a safe price); realistic agentic workloads sit around 0.6–0.8, wide enough that a meaningful share of tasks blow straight through a mean-based price.

The blue curve is the cost-per-task distribution (log-normal — the standard model for right-skewed token consumption). Crank the CoV up and watch the tail stretch.
The red line is the price if you set it off the mean cost (plus your markup). The shaded red area to its right is every run that costs more than that price — pure loss.
The green line is the P90 floor (P90 cost × 1.15). Almost the entire distribution sits to its left, so very few runs lose money.

The Monte-Carlo engine simulates 20,000 individual tasks and 800 months on every change. Notice that with a realistic CoV (0.6–0.8), pricing at the mean leaves you underwater on roughly 40% of tasks — the number from the lecture, now live.

Rule of thumb: the higher the CoV, the more the mean lies to you. Above CoV ≈ 0.7, set the M5 floor on the P95 monthly cost, not 60–80% of the M4 base.

title: M5 Outcome Designer
text:
An M5 fee is never simply “a percent of value.” It’s a clamped — and ideally tiered — function:
\[\text{Fee} = \max\big(\text{Floor},\ \min(\text{Ceiling},\ \text{Value} \times \text{Share}\%)\big)\]
Set the floor, ceiling, and share below, then watch the fee curve. The lesson lands fast: a flat share looks fine at small value but becomes a renegotiation magnet at scale — a tiered (Lehman-style) schedule stays durable.

title: M5 Outcome Designer
text:
Design the deal

// Every viewof below is wrapped in this so hovering shows a native browser
// tooltip specific to that input — same approach as comparator.qmd.
withDescription = (input, text) => { input.title = text; return input; }






Cost-plus inputs — the cost-recovery basis the floor is built from:

viewof m4base   = withDescription(Inputs.range([2000, 40000], {value: 10000, step: 500,  label: "Equivalent M4 base fee (£/mo)"}),
  "Not an M5 fee itself — this is what M4 would charge for the same engagement, used only to derive the floor below.")
viewof floorPct = withDescription(Inputs.range([0.6, 0.8],     {value: 0.8,   step: 0.05, label: "Floor (× M4 base)"}),
  "Floor = this × the M4 base fee above. Protects cost recovery — the fee can never drop below this, regardless of how the flat/tiered share and value combine.")















Value inputs — what the deal is worth, and the share of it the fee captures:

viewof valueType = withDescription(Inputs.select([
  "Cost takeout (labour replaced)",
  "Cost avoidance (fraud, penalties)",
  "Revenue uplift (attributed)",
  "Risk reduction (liability avoided)"
], {label: "Value type", value: "Cost takeout (labour replaced)"}),
  "What kind of value this fee is a share of. Doesn't change the calculation below — it's descriptive, framing which real-world verifiability questions apply to this deal.")
viewof flatShare = withDescription(Inputs.range([0.01, 0.06], {value: 0.03,  step: 0.005, label: "Flat share %"}),
  "% of expected value charged under the flat-share model — the one this whole page argues against once value scales.")
viewof expValue  = withDescription(Inputs.range([0, 5000000], {value: 1000000, step: 50000, label: "Expected monthly value (£)"}),
  "Expected monthly value the engagement creates. Drives both the flat-share and tiered fee curves below.")






















Risk / guardrail inputs — caps the customer’s exposure (and the vendor’s renegotiation risk) at scale:

viewof ceilMult = withDescription(Inputs.range([3, 5], {value: 4, step: 0.5, label: "Ceiling (× floor)"}),
  "Caps the fee at this multiple of the floor. Guards against renegotiation risk if value scales a long way past what was priced for.")







viewof useTiered = withDescription(Inputs.toggle({value: true, label: "Show tiered (Lehman) schedule"}),
  "Toggle between a flat % share (one rate, whole value) and the tiered Lehman-style schedule below (declining rate by band).")












Tiered (Lehman) schedule — edit the steps





What is “Lehman tiering”? It’s named after the classic Lehman Formula, the declining-rate fee scale investment banks have long used for M&A advisory success fees (the original 1960s Lehman Brothers rule of thumb was 5% of the first $1M, 4% of the next, 3% of the next, and so on down to 1%). The mechanism is simple: instead of one flat percentage applied to the whole pool of value, the value is split into bands, and each successive band is charged at a lower rate than the one before it.
Applied to outcome-based AI pricing, it solves the exact problem a flat share creates: a flat % feels fair on a modest deal, but multiply it across a huge value pool and the fee balloons into what looks like a windfall — inviting renegotiation, or worse, a reputation for opportunistic pricing. Tiering the rate downward as value climbs keeps the vendor’s take proportionate at every scale, so the deal that looked fair at signing still looks fair a year later when the customer’s usage has 10×’d. Below, the three bands (t1rate down through t3rate) default to a 4% / 2.5% / 1% schedule — edit them to see how the fee curve bends.

viewof t1rate = withDescription(Inputs.range([0.01, 0.06], {value: 0.04,  step: 0.005, label: "Rate on first band"}),
  "Highest of the three rates — charged on value up to the first band's cap below.")
viewof t1cap  = withDescription(Inputs.range([100000, 1000000], {value: 500000, step: 50000, label: "First band up to (£/mo)"}),
  "Value up to this point is charged at the first (highest) rate above.")
viewof t2rate = withDescription(Inputs.range([0.01, 0.05], {value: 0.025, step: 0.005, label: "Rate on second band"}),
  "Middle rate — charged on the slice of value between the first and second band caps.")
viewof t2cap  = withDescription(Inputs.range([1000000, 3000000], {value: 2000000, step: 100000, label: "Second band up to (£/mo)"}),
  "Value between the first cap and this point is charged at the second rate above.")
viewof t3rate = withDescription(Inputs.range([0.005, 0.03],{value: 0.01,  step: 0.005, label: "Rate above second band"}),
  "Lowest of the three rates — charged on any value above the second band's cap, keeping the fee proportionate at very large scale.")








































chartMax = 5000000

floor   = m4base * floorPct
ceiling = ceilMult * floor

clamp = (x) => Math.max(floor, Math.min(ceiling, x))

flatRaw   = (v) => v * flatShare
tieredRaw = (v) => t1rate * Math.min(v, t1cap)
                 + t2rate * Math.max(0, Math.min(v, t2cap) - t1cap)
                 + t3rate * Math.max(0, v - t2cap)

flatFee   = (v) => clamp(flatRaw(v))
tieredFee = (v) => clamp(tieredRaw(v))

binding = (raw) => raw <= floor ? "floor binds" : raw >= ceiling ? "ceiling binds" : "share applies"

shareBand = ({
  "Cost takeout (labour replaced)":     "3–5%",
  "Cost avoidance (fraud, penalties)":  "2–4%",
  "Revenue uplift (attributed)":        "2–4%",
  "Risk reduction (liability avoided)": "2–5%"
})[valueType]

gbp  = (x) => "£" + Math.round(x).toLocaleString("en-GB")
gbpC = (x) => x >= 1e6 ? "£" + (x/1e6).toFixed(x >= 1e7 ? 0 : 2) + "M"
            : x >= 1e3 ? "£" + Math.round(x/1e3) + "k" : "£" + Math.round(x)
axisFmt = (s) => s >= 1e6 ? "£" + (s/1e6) + "M" : s >= 1e3 ? "£" + (s/1e3) + "k" : "£" + s
pct  = (x) => (100*x).toFixed(1) + "%"

curve = {
  const n = 240, a = [];
  for (let i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
    const v = chartMax * i / n;
    a.push({v, fee: flatFee(v), series: "Flat share"});
    if (useTiered) a.push({v, fee: tieredFee(v), series: "Tiered (Lehman)"});
  }
  return a;
}

effCurve = {
  const n = 240, a = [];
  for (let i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
    const v = chartMax * i / n;
    a.push({v, eff: 100 * flatFee(v) / v, series: "Flat share"});
    if (useTiered) a.push({v, eff: 100 * tieredFee(v) / v, series: "Tiered (Lehman)"});
  }
  return a;
}

palette = ({"Flat share": "#C0392B", "Tiered (Lehman)": "#4AA82D"})

opPoints = useTiered
  ? [{v: expValue, fee: flatFee(expValue), series: "Flat share"},
     {v: expValue, fee: tieredFee(expValue), series: "Tiered (Lehman)"}]
  : [{v: expValue, fee: flatFee(expValue), series: "Flat share"}]
































































































































html`<div style="font-size:.9em;color:#555;margin:-.3em 0 .4em;">
  Recommended share for <b>${valueType}</b>: <b>${shareBand}</b>.
  Floor = ${gbp(floor)}/mo · Ceiling = ${gbp(ceiling)}/mo.</div>`

title: M5 Outcome Designer
text:
Fee vs. value delivered

Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 70, marginTop: 30, marginBottom: 40, height: 360,
  x: {label: "Monthly value delivered →", tickFormat: axisFmt, grid: true},
  y: {label: "↑ Monthly fee to Vendor", tickFormat: axisFmt, grid: true,
      // Headroom so the "ceiling ..." label above the plateaued line isn't clipped.
      domain: [0, ceiling * 1.18]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: Object.keys(palette), range: Object.values(palette)},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleY([floor],   {stroke: "#888", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.ruleY([ceiling], {stroke: "#00005C", strokeDasharray: "4 3"}),
    Plot.text([{y: floor, t: "floor " + gbpC(floor)}],
      {x: 0, y: "y", text: "t", textAnchor: "start", dy: -5, fill: "#888", fontSize: 11}),
    Plot.text([{y: ceiling, t: "ceiling " + gbpC(ceiling)}],
      {x: 0, y: "y", text: "t", textAnchor: "start", dy: -5, fill: "#00005C", fontSize: 11}),
    Plot.line(curve, {x: "v", y: "fee", stroke: "series", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([expValue], {stroke: "#bbb", strokeDasharray: "2 2"}),
    Plot.dot(opPoints, {x: "v", y: "fee", fill: "series", r: 5, stroke: "white"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})

title: M5 Outcome Designer
M5 Outcome Designer
M5 Outcome Designer
section: Effective share — why flat doesn’t scale
text:
Effective share — why flat doesn’t scale

Plot.plot({
  marginLeft: 50, marginBottom: 40, height: 300,
  x: {label: "Monthly value delivered →", tickFormat: axisFmt, grid: true},
  y: {label: "↑ effective share (fee ÷ value)", tickFormat: d => d + "%", grid: true,
      domain: [0, Math.max(flatShare, t1rate) * 100 * 1.25]},
  color: {legend: true, domain: Object.keys(palette), range: Object.values(palette)},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(effCurve, {x: "v", y: "eff", stroke: "series", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([expValue], {stroke: "#bbb", strokeDasharray: "2 2"}),
    Plot.ruleY([0])
  ]
})






The flat line stays constant until the ceiling clips it, then decays. The tiered line steps down smoothly — capturing more where Vendor contribution is proportionally highest (low-to-mid value) and compressing where the customer’s own operational context dominates. That declining curve is exactly what makes a tiered schedule feel fair, and survive renewal.






Illustrative





Constants teach the shape, not a real deal. M5 also requires L4 autonomy, an audited baseline, E&O insurance, and CoE Director approval — see the Model Selector.

title: Agentic AI Pricing Lab
text:
In the lecture we opened with a puzzle:

You build an agent that reviews contracts. It does the work of three paralegals. It costs you £200 a month to run. A law firm pays £180,000 a year for those people. So… what do you charge?

The point of that puzzle was that there is no single answer. The same piece of software can be priced anywhere from “cost plus a little” to “a share of the value it unlocks” — a spread of 100× or more — depending only on the commercial model you choose and the risk you take on.
These pages let you drive the models yourself. Move the sliders, watch the price move, and build the intuition that the framework tries to capture.






Everything here runs in your browser



There is no server. The calculators run as code inside this page, so you can fork the site, change the formulas, and host your own version on GitHub Pages for free.

  %% Blank spacer nodes below each cluster title, invisibly linked to the
  %% first real node — Mermaid otherwise renders that node's box right under
  %% the cluster title text, overlapping it, especially when the node also
  %% has an incoming edge from outside the cluster pulling it upward.
  subgraph EXT["External / qualitative drivers"]
    extSpacer[" "]
    complexity["Task / workflow<br/>complexity"]
    autonomyQ["Autonomy level<br/>(L1–L5)"]
    riskQ["Risk score<br/>(1–10)"]
    tier["Deployment tier<br/>(1 / 2 / 3)"]
    extSpacer ~~~ complexity
  end

  subgraph SHARED["Shared engagement inputs"]
    sharedSpacer[" "]
    fte["FTE count × FTE cost"]
    vol["Volume<br/>(tasks delivered/mo)"]
    val["Business value<br/>created (£/mo)"]
    sharedSpacer ~~~ fte
  end

  subgraph TOKENS["Token-cost model<br/>(M2 T2 & M3, set independently)"]
    tokensSpacer[" "]
    cov["Token CoV"]
    meanC["Mean token cost"]
    p90C["P90 token cost"]
    tokensSpacer ~~~ cov
    cov --> meanC
    cov --> p90C
  end

  style extSpacer fill:transparent,stroke:none
  style sharedSpacer fill:transparent,stroke:none
  style tokensSpacer fill:transparent,stroke:none

  tier -->|filters models| models["Active models<br/>(§5.4 mapping)"]
  tier -->|picks formula| m2choice["M2: Tier 1 vs Tier 2"]

  riskQ --> overlayN["overlay()<br/>M1, M2 T1, M4 only"]

  riskQ -.->|not wired| ownRisk["M2 T2 / M3<br/>risk premium"]

  complexity -.->|not wired| cov

title: Causal Map
section: From drivers to price, cost & margin
text:
From drivers to price, cost & margin





%%{init: {"theme": "base", "themeVariables": {"fontSize": "16px", "primaryColor": "#eaf1fb", "primaryBorderColor": "#4a6fa5", "primaryTextColor": "#1a1a1a", "lineColor": "#7a7a7a"}, "flowchart": {"nodeSpacing": 35, "rankSpacing": 55}}}%%
flowchart TB
  overlayN2["overlay() output"] --> m1price["M1 price"]
  overlayN2 --> m2t1price["M2 T1 price"]
  overlayN2 --> m4price["M4 price"]

  vol2["Volume"] --> m3price2["M3 price<br/>= volume × task price"]
  vol2 -->|"× calls/task"| m2calls["M2 T2<br/>effective calls"]
  meanC2["Mean token cost"] --> m2price2["M2 T2 unit price<br/>(quoted)"]
  m2calls --> m2price2
  p90C2["P90 token cost"] --> m2cost2["M2 T2 cost<br/>(for margin)"]
  m2calls --> m2cost2
  p90C2 --> m3cost2["M3 cost<br/>(for margin)"]
  vol2 --> m3cost2

  val2["Business value"] --> m4price
  m4price -->|"0.8 × base"| floor2["M5 floor"]
  p90C2 -.->|"not wired — see gap below"| floor2
  floor2 --> m5price2["M5 price"]
  val2 --> m5price2

  humanBase2["Human cost baseline"] -.-> sanity2["M3 sanity check"]
  m3price2 --> sanity2
  vol2 --> sanity2

  m1price & m2t1price & m2price2 & m2cost2 & m3price2 & m3cost2 & m4price & m5price2 --> chart2["Bar chart:<br/>price / cost / profit / margin"]
